title: The Hive Switch
coreMove: Notice the cues that move people from private calculation into shared-body coordination.
sourcePressure: The chapter explains conditions under which people shift into group-minded coordination through the hive switch.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer makes the hive switch mystical or turns it into ordinary crowd pressure.

sourceAnchors.name: the hive switch
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar treats the hive switch as the mechanism for shifting from self to group-minded coordination.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The hive switch is the moment the private self loosens and the group starts to feel like the larger body.

sourceAnchors.name: selfish-versus-groupish tension
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says Chapter 10 builds directly on Chapter 9's selfish-versus-groupish tension.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The switch matters because the same person who guards a private advantage can suddenly guard the group as if it were personal.

hook: Do not open ch10 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: rowing crew finding rhythm after weeks of individual correction
exampleSpecs.audience: coaches watching coordination become shared attention
exampleSpecs.stakes: Ben spots the moment eight private efforts become one stroke.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben stops shouting technique and lets the crew hear the catch timing until they synchronize.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Oarlocks click out of order across the gray water.

exampleSpecs.domain: warehouse safety team using synchronized shutdown drills
exampleSpecs.audience: operations teams trying to make safety collective
exampleSpecs.stakes: Astrid turns a rule into a shared ritual with a visible group cue.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Astrid starts the same red-light shutdown drill at every bay and watches workers move together.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A red light washes over stacked pallets in six loading bays.

exampleSpecs.domain: music festival volunteers forming trust before gates open
exampleSpecs.audience: event leads managing strangers under pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: Aman uses shared timing and call-response to create group readiness.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Aman has volunteers practice the same gate call until strangers answer as one team.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "When I say blue gate, you answer clear," Aman tells forty strangers.

exampleSpecs.domain: surgical unit preparing for a mass-casualty drill
exampleSpecs.audience: medical teams that need coordinated mode shift
exampleSpecs.stakes: Isabel notices the switch when names give way to roles.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 6:40, Isabel calls the role drill and watches private chatter disappear into coordinated tasks.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 6:40, Isabel hears the trauma bay go quiet before the drill starts.

exampleSpecs.domain: tenant association cleaning a neglected courtyard
exampleSpecs.audience: neighbors who barely know each other
exampleSpecs.stakes: Ryan sees shared labor turn complaint into group identity.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ryan compares the meeting minutes with the morning when everyone picked up tools together.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Ryan one Saturday with rented rakes to hear people say our courtyard.

exampleSpecs.domain: software security team during a live breach exercise
exampleSpecs.audience: engineers moving from solo expertise to coordinated defense
exampleSpecs.stakes: Anke creates a common pulse through timed status calls and shared risk.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What changes when Anke makes every defender answer on the same thirty-second cadence?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What if the fix is not more expertise but a shared pulse?

skillTargets: identify cues that activate group-minded coordination
distinguish hive-switch absorption from simple conformity
explain why shared motion or risk can change self-boundaries

tryThisNowSpec: Name one setting where you feel absorbed into a group, then identify the cue: synchronized movement, shared risk, music, chant, or ritual.
